what: Super Group runs online betting and casino brands. Its main brand is Betway, a sports betting operation active in many countries, alongside Spin, an online casino business. Customers place bets and play casino games through its apps and websites, and the company keeps the margin between stakes and payouts.
customers: Online sports bettors and casino players across Europe, Africa, Canada and other regulated markets, reached through heavy marketing and sports sponsorships.
money: Margin on sports bets placed through Betway across many countries.
Margin on casino games through Spin and related brands.
moat: Online gambling is a marketing and licensing business: brand recognition brings customers, and local licences restrict who may compete. Super Group’s advantage is geographic breadth — it operates across many regulated markets rather than depending on one — plus the technology and payments infrastructure to handle many currencies and regulatory regimes at once.
risks: Gambling regulation can change abruptly in any market: advertising bans, stake limits, tax increases and outright prohibition have all happened and can remove a market’s profitability overnight.
Ten analysts average a $17.20 target against a $10.55 price, a 63% gap reflecting very different views on regulatory risk.
Customer acquisition costs are high and competitive, and marketing must continue indefinitely to replace churning customers.
Revenue depends partly on sporting results, because unusual outcomes can produce a quarter of poor betting margins.
Gambling carries genuine social harm, and public and political pressure to restrict it has been increasing in many markets.
opportunities: Revenue has grown consistently, from $1.5B in 2021 to $2.2B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $2.5B.
The shares trade at about 13.0 times earnings, 7.8 times EV/EBITDA and 2.2 times sales.
Cash of $387.4M against essentially no debt is an unusually clean balance sheet.
Operating across many regulated markets means no single regulatory change can destroy the business.
Online gambling continues to take share from betting shops and physical casinos in most markets.
watch: Active customers and revenue per customer by region. Growth in this industry is bought with marketing, so the cost of acquiring customers against what they generate is the only economics that matter.
view: Online gambling is one of the most profitable consumer businesses in existence and one of the most politically exposed, and Super Group illustrates both. The economics are excellent: there is no inventory, no physical premises, and the margin between stakes and payouts is mathematically assured over enough bets. Revenue has grown from $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion trailing, with $387 million of cash and essentially no debt, which is an unusually clean position for this industry.

The geographic breadth is the strategic feature worth understanding. Super Group operates Betway and Spin across many regulated markets — Europe, Africa, Canada and others — rather than concentrating on one. That matters because the single largest risk in this industry is a regulator changing the rules: advertising bans, deposit limits, stake caps, tax increases and outright prohibition have all happened somewhere, and a company dependent on one market can lose most of its value in a single legislative session. Breadth converts a company-ending risk into a bad quarter.

What breadth does not solve is the direction of political sentiment. Public concern about gambling harm has been rising in most developed markets, and the regulatory trend is consistently toward restriction rather than liberalisation. That is a structural headwind on profitability across the whole industry, and it is the main reason gambling companies trade at single-digit EV/EBITDA multiples while other businesses with these economics do not.

At 13 times earnings and 7.8 times EV/EBITDA, with no debt, the price is undemanding and the ten analysts averaging 63% above it reflect how differently people weigh the regulation. The operating variable to follow is active customers and revenue per customer by region, because growth in this industry is bought with marketing and the question is always whether a customer generates more than they cost to acquire. A company whose revenue is growing while acquisition spending grows faster is not actually growing.
bull: Geographic breadth absorbs any single regulator’s crackdown while online keeps taking share from physical betting, and a debt-free business at 7.8 times EV/EBITDA compounds.
bear: Regulatory restriction spreads across multiple markets at once, customer acquisition costs keep rising, and political pressure on gambling permanently compresses the multiple.
